beginner: Figs are not fussy about soil and grow in a wide range, from sandy to heavier ground, as long as it drains well and does not stay soggy. A loam with some organic matter is ideal, but figs even do fine in poor, rocky soil. The one thing to avoid is sandy soil that is full of root-knot nematodes, tiny soil pests that are the leading killer of figs. Do not make the soil too rich either: too much rich material and feeding pushes soft leafy growth and fewer figs, and that soft growth is more easily hurt by winter cold.
seasoned: Fig is adaptable across soil textures, from sandy to clay loam, provided drainage is good; it tolerates poor and rocky ground better than most fruit trees. A well-drained loam with moderate organic matter is ideal. The critical avoidance is root-knot-nematode-infested sandy soil, which is the leading cause of fig decline in warm regions, since own-rooted figs carry no resistant rootstock. Keep fertility moderate: over-rich soil and heavy feeding drive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and produce soft wood that is more prone to winter injury.

beginner: Figs do best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, but they are easygoing and grow well anywhere from about 6.0 up to 7.8 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and only adjust if it is far off: garden lime raises a too-acidic pH and elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Mix any amendment in before you plant.
seasoned: Fig prefers a slightly acidic soil near pH 6.0 to 6.5 but is tolerant across roughly 6.0 to 7.8, handling near-neutral ground without trouble. Test before planting and correct only a real deficiency: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers an alkaline one. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to set before the permanent plant goes in.

beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Figs need much less than other fruit trees, and too much does more harm than good: lots of leaves and few figs, split fruit, and soft growth that is easily hurt by winter cold. Scatter a balanced fertilizer around the plant out to where the branches reach, keep it off the stems, and water it in. In colder areas use half as much, and stop feeding by midsummer so the plant can toughen up before winter.
seasoned: Feed lightly. Figs need far less fertilizer than most fruit trees, and over-feeding is a common mistake: excess nitrogen pushes rank leafy growth, delays and reduces fruiting, can cause fruit to split, and produces soft wood that winters poorly. Broadcast a balanced granular evenly around the root zone out toward the drip line, keep it off the stems, and water it in. Halve the rate in colder regions to favor hardiness, and never feed past midsummer, since late nitrogen keeps the plant growing when it should be hardening for winter.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all a fig needs. Do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, because too much gives you leaves instead of figs.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 suits figs; they are light feeders and need no high-nitrogen program. Too much nitrogen (N) is counterproductive, driving leaves over fruit and reducing cold hardiness.

beginner: A simple guide is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young fig and 2 to 4 pounds for a big one, spread over 2 or 3 times from early spring to early summer. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until it starts growing. In cold-winter areas, use half as much.
seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young plant and 2 to 4 pounds for a mature one, split into 2 or 3 applications from early spring through early summer; UGA gives a rule of about 1/2 pound per foot of height, up to 5 pounds a year. Do not fertilize at planting; wait until growth begins. Cut these rates in half in northern gardens to keep growth firm for winter.

beginner: Figs make fruit on their own with no pollination, so you do not need any companion plants to help them fruit. What matters for a fig is what happens around its roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back and lay down mulch to hold moisture and keep weeds down, and do not plant a fig in soil full of root-knot nematodes (tiny soil pests), because figs cannot fight them off. A mulched, weed-free, pest-free root area is really all a fig asks for.
seasoned: Fig is parthenocarpic and self-fruitful, so there are no pollination companions to plant: a lone tree fruits with no bees and no fig wasp. The interactions that matter for a fig are at the root zone, not classic vegetable pairings. Keep grass and weeds cleared back and mulch the root area, which competes down weeds and holds moisture, and above all keep the plant out of soil heavily infested with root-knot nematodes, which own-rooted figs cannot resist. A well-mulched, weed-free, nematode-free root zone is the whole companion story.

beginner: The fig slowly goes downhill for no obvious reason: stunted, with thin yellow leaves, dieback, and fewer figs each year. If you dig up a root, you find small knots or swellings on it. Those knots are the damage from the pest.
seasoned: Above ground, a slow, unexplained decline: stunted growth, sparse yellowing leaves, dieback, and poor fruiting that worsens over years. Below ground, the roots carry small knots or galls, and the fine feeder roots are damaged, so the plant cannot take up water and nutrients.

beginner: Microscopic soil worms called root-knot nematodes that live in the roots and make the knots. They build up in warm, sandy soil and are the number-one killer of figs in warm areas. Because figs grow on their own roots, there is no special root you can buy to resist them and no cure once a plant is badly infested.
seasoned: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species), microscopic soil roundworms that feed inside the roots and form the galls. They build up in warm, sandy soils and are the leading cause of fig decline and death in the Southeast and other warm sandy regions. Own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock, so there is no cure once a plant is heavily infested.

beginner: Once a plant is badly infested there is no fix. The best you can do is keep the fig strong with steady water and a thick mulch so it can shrug off mild damage, and, in bad sandy soil, grow it in a pot of clean potting mix instead of in the ground.
seasoned: There is no rescue treatment for an infested plant. Manage it by keeping the fig vigorous and well watered so it outgrows light damage, mulching heavily to build soil organic matter and beneficial soil life, and, in the worst sandy sites, growing in a container of clean mix instead. A thick organic mulch is the practical home tool.

beginner: The main thing is to avoid the problem: do not plant in sandy soil known to have these pests, pick well-drained ground, mulch thickly, and keep the fig healthy. Where the soil is bad, growing the fig in a pot of clean mix avoids the pest completely.
seasoned: Prevention is everything: do not plant into known nematode-heavy sandy soil, choose the best-drained ground, mulch heavily, and keep the plant vigorous. Where nematode pressure is high, container culture in clean mix sidesteps the problem entirely.

beginner: Ripe figs turn sour and mushy inside, with a fizzy or scummy ooze coming out of the little hole at the bottom (the eye) and a vinegary smell. You may see tiny beetles around the soft fruit. The affected figs are ruined.
seasoned: Ripening figs ferment and sour from the inside, oozing a scummy or bubbly liquid from the eye and smelling vinegary or yeasty. Small beetles may be seen at the eye of soft fruit. Affected figs are inedible and drop or rot on the plant.

beginner: Little beetles called dried fruit beetles are attracted to ripe figs and carry the yeasts that cause souring into the fruit through the open hole at the bottom. It is worst in humid weather and on figs with a big open eye that lets the beetles in.
seasoned: Dried fruit beetles (Carpophilus species) and other sap beetles are drawn to ripe figs and carry souring yeasts and bacteria into the fruit through the open eye. The problem is worst in humid weather and on varieties with a large, open eye, which lets the beetles and moisture in.

beginner: Pick figs as soon as they are ripe and clean up any soured or fallen fruit right away, so the beetles are not attracted and the souring cannot spread. Growing a variety with a small, tight eye like Celeste helps a lot. No spray fixes souring once it is inside the fig.
seasoned: Pick figs promptly as they ripen and remove any soured or dropped fruit right away so beetles are not drawn in and the yeasts do not build. Choosing varieties with a small or closed eye (such as Celeste) greatly reduces souring. There is no spray that reaches yeasts inside the fruit.

beginner: Keep the figs picked and throw away any soured ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your summers are humid. Picking often and keeping the plant open are the best defenses.
seasoned: Keep the plant picked clean during ripening, dispose of soured fruit, and favor closed-eye varieties in humid areas. Good airflow and prompt harvest are the durable controls.

beginner: Ripe figs get pecked open, half-eaten, or disappear, usually the best ones up high first. Squirrels can strip a small fig fast. It happens right as the figs start to ripen.
seasoned: Ripe and nearly ripe figs are pecked open, half-eaten, or gone entirely, often the best fruit at the top of the plant first. Squirrels strip fruit and can clear a small tree fast. Damage appears exactly as the crop begins to ripen.

beginner: Birds and squirrels love ripe figs, and because a fig's fruit is soft, sweet, and out in the open for weeks, they come back again and again. It is one of the most common fig problems.
seasoned: Birds and squirrels find ripe figs irresistible, and a fig's soft, sweet, unprotected fruit ripening over many weeks is an easy, repeated target. This is one of the most common complaints of home fig growers.

beginner: The best fix is to drape bird netting over the plant as the figs start to color, and to pick ripe figs often so fewer are left hanging. Shiny tape or scare items help for a while. A potted fig can be moved somewhere more protected.
seasoned: Netting the plant (or key branches) as fruit begins to color is the most effective home control; pick ripe figs promptly and often so less hangs waiting. Reflective tape and scare devices help briefly. A container fig can be moved to a more protected spot.

beginner: Get the netting ready before the figs ripen, not after the birds find them, and keep the plant small enough to cover and pick easily.
seasoned: Plan for netting before the crop ripens rather than after the losses start, and keep the plant a manageable size so it can be covered and picked easily.

beginner: In late summer, leaves get small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly underneath, and then yellow and fall early, sometimes stripping the plant before fall. That year's figs usually still ripen, but losing leaves early year after year wears the plant down.
seasoned: In mid to late summer, leaves develop small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty reddish-brown, most on the underside; heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop early, sometimes defoliating the plant well before fall. The current crop usually still ripens, but repeated early defoliation weakens the plant over years.

beginner: A fungus called Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, wet, humid weather and survives winter on fallen infected leaves, so it is worst in humid areas and wet summers, especially where old leaves pile up under the plant.
seasoned: The fungus Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, humid, wet weather and overwinters on fallen infected leaves, so it is most severe in the humid Southeast and in wet summers, building up where litter is left under the plant.

beginner: Once a leaf is spotted you cannot cure it; the aim is to slow it down and protect next year. Rake up and throw away fallen leaves, and keep the plant open so it dries fast. Where rust is bad, an organic copper spray on the new leaves through the season is the usual treatment.
seasoned: Once leaves are spotted there is no cure for that leaf; the goal is to slow the spread and protect next year. Rake up and destroy fallen leaves to remove the overwintering source, and keep the canopy open and dry. Where rust is severe, a neutral copper or Bordeaux fungicide on the new foliage through the growing season is the standard organic option.

beginner: The main prevention is cleanup: rake away fallen leaves every year, prune so air moves through the plant, and water the ground instead of the leaves. In humid areas where rust is common, an organic copper spray starting in spring keeps the leaves protected.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: clear fallen leaves each year, prune for airflow, and water at the ground rather than overhead. In rust-prone humid regions, a preventive copper program from spring protects the foliage.

beginner: Leaves get a blotchy, mottled yellow pattern (called a mosaic), and sometimes the fruit is spotted or drops early. It comes and goes with the season and variety. It does not kill the plant, but it can slow it down and cut the crop.
seasoned: Leaves show scattered yellow, blotchy, or ring-like mottling (a mosaic pattern), sometimes with distorted growth; fruit may be spotted or drop early. Symptoms vary with season and variety and often come and go. The virus does not kill the plant but can reduce vigor and crop.

beginner: Fig mosaic is a virus, spread mostly by a tiny mite (the fig mite) and passed along in cuttings from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is in the plant for good, because there is no cure for a plant virus.
seasoned: Fig mosaic is a virus complex spread mainly by the tiny fig mite (Aceria ficus) and carried in cuttings taken from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is systemic and permanent, since there is no cure for a virus in a plant.

beginner: There is no cure for a plant virus. Just keep the fig healthy and well cared for, since many infected plants still fruit alright. Do not take cuttings from a mottled plant to start new ones, and pull out a plant that is badly stunted and barely fruiting.
seasoned: There is no treatment for a virus in a plant. Manage it by keeping the plant otherwise healthy and vigorous; many infected figs still crop acceptably. Do not propagate cuttings from a mottled plant, and remove a severely stunted, poor-cropping plant.

beginner: The best prevention is starting with a healthy plant and controlling the tiny fig mites that spread it. Buy or take cuttings from plants with clean, un-mottled leaves. There is no way to cure a plant once it is infected.
seasoned: Prevention is about clean stock and mite control: start with cuttings or plants from healthy, unmottled sources, and keep fig mites in check since they spread the virus. There is no way to cure an infected plant.

beginner: Figs rot from the inside near the little hole at the bottom, going brown and mushy inside even when the outside still looks okay, then souring and dropping. It goes hand in hand with the souring that beetles cause, and is worst in humid weather on figs with a big open eye.
seasoned: Ripening fruit rots from the inside near the eye, turning brown and mushy internally while the outside may still look sound; affected figs sour, ooze, and drop. It overlaps with beetle-spread souring and is worst in humid weather on open-eye varieties.

beginner: A rot inside the fruit caused by fungi that get in through the open hole at the bottom, often carried by the same little beetles that cause souring. Humid weather and big-eye varieties make it worse.
seasoned: An internal fruit rot caused by fungi (including Fusarium) carried into the fruit through the open eye, often by the same sap beetles that spread souring. Humid conditions and large-eye varieties make it worse.

beginner: You cannot cure it inside the fruit. Handle it like souring: pick figs promptly, throw away rotten and dropped ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your area is humid.
seasoned: There is no in-fruit cure. Control it the same way as souring: pick promptly, remove affected and dropped fruit, and favor small or closed-eye varieties (such as Celeste) in humid areas.

beginner: Grow a tight-eye variety in humid areas, keep the figs picked and the ground clean, and control the little beetles that carry it.
seasoned: Choose closed-eye varieties in humid regions, keep fruit picked and the ground clean, and manage the sap beetles that carry the fungi.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week from rain or the hose during the growing season, more when it is hot or the soil is sandy. A new fig needs steady water while it gets its roots going. An older fig can take some dry spells, but the figs come out small and less sweet if it gets too dry.
seasoned: Water deeply and regularly rather than lightly and often: figure roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week from rain or irrigation through the growing season, more in heat and sandy soil, easing off as fruit finishes and through winter dormancy. A newly planted fig needs the most attention while it roots in; an established fig is fairly drought-tolerant but sizes and sweetens fruit poorly when it runs dry.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches the roots, not just a splash on top. A new fig wants about 10 gallons per soak, two or three times a week its first summer. An older, fruiting fig wants roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, and more when it is hot.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing fig, UF/IFAS suggests around 10 gallons per soak two to three times a week in the first season; for a bearing plant, aim for the equivalent of about 1 to 1.5 inches per week through the growing season, more in heat.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and try to keep the leaves and fruit dry, since wet leaves invite disease. Keep the watering steady while the figs are filling out and ripening, because going from dry to very wet, or a hard rain on ripe figs, makes them split and spoil.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the drip line, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and fruit souring. Keep moisture especially steady as the fruit sizes and ripens, since a swing from dry to soaked (or heavy rain on ripening figs) causes fruit to split and sour.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that stays soggy, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a plant slowly going downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. Figs handle moisture better than a peach but still cannot sit in waterlogged soil. Figs that split and sour after a lot of water or rain are another sign near harvest.
seasoned: Chronically wet, poorly drained soil shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and general decline as waterlogged roots suffocate. Figs tolerate more moisture than stone fruit but still fail in standing water. Fruit that splits and sours after heavy watering or rain is the other overwatering signal near harvest.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull yellow leaves, leaves dropping early, and, most clearly, small figs falling off or ripening tiny and less sweet. A fig that gets too dry in summer drops some of its fruit, so try to catch the dryness before the figs suffer.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull and yellowing leaves, early leaf drop, and, most tellingly, fruit that drops while small or ripens undersized and less sweet. A fig short of water during the summer swell aborts part of its crop, so catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the fig is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 10 gallons two or three times a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow strong roots.
seasoned: Through the first season keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of roughly 10 gallons two to three times a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the root system the plant relies on later.

beginner: While the figs are filling out, keep the water steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week as deep soaks. Even watering now means bigger, sweeter figs, and it keeps the fruit from splitting.
seasoned: As the main crop sizes, keep moisture steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches per week as deep soaks. This is the window where even watering translates directly into fuller, sweeter figs and where a dry-then-wet swing causes fruit to split and sour.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the fig is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the fig is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells so roots do not desiccate. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give the fig a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground instead of over the top, since wet leaves and fruit invite disease. Young figs need steady water the first season. Older figs handle dry spells, but they drop figs when too dry and split them when a dry spell ends in a big soak or rain.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and souring. Young figs need consistent moisture through the first season to establish; mature figs are moderately drought-tolerant but drop and undersize fruit under stress, and split when a dry spell breaks in heavy water or rain.

beginner: Fill the pot with a good-quality potting mix that drains well. A bark-based mix, or a general potting soil with some extra perlite stirred in, works nicely. Figs are not picky, but avoid a heavy soil dug from the yard, which packs down and drains poorly in a pot.
seasoned: Use a quality bark-based or peat-based potting mix amended for drainage, not native garden soil, which compacts under container irrigation. Figs tolerate a more moisture-retentive mix than stone fruit but still perform best with free drainage and an air-filled root zone.

seasoned: Blend in modest compost for fertility and extra perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive. Figs accept richer container media than most fruit trees, but keep drainage the priority; a top-dress of compost each spring covers most of the plant's needs.

beginner: A fig in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. Water more often than a ground fig, but do not leave the pot standing in a saucer of water. In winter, when the plant is resting, give it just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
seasoned: A potted fig dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. Water more often, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer. Through dormancy the plant needs only enough water to keep the root ball from drying out.

Do not feed at planting, and stop once it drops its leaves for winter.
seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into fall. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely once the plant goes dormant.

beginner: Growing a fig in a pot is the easiest way to keep one where winters are too cold for it in the ground, because you can move it somewhere protected. Before hard freezes come, move the pot into an unheated but sheltered spot like an attached garage, shed, or basement that stays cold but does not deep-freeze. The fig is leafless and resting, so it does not need light in there. Water it just once in a while so the roots do not dry out, and bring it back outside when hard frosts are past in spring.
seasoned: A container is the standard way to carry a fig through winters colder than its in-ground range. Once the plant is dormant and leafless, move the pot to an unheated but protected space (attached garage, shed, or cool basement) that holds above roughly the mid teens but stays cold enough to keep it dormant. It needs no light while leafless; water sparingly to keep the root ball from drying out. Return it outdoors after hard frosts pass. A container fig still needs its short winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

Expect a smaller plant and a lighter but dependable crop.

beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not the best choice for a fig. Figs do best when the soil dries out a bit between waterings, and a tank keeps the roots wet all the time, which can cause root trouble and split fruit. Figs handle moisture better than a peach, so it can work if that is what you have, but a regular pot that drains well and that you water yourself grows better figs.
seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not the best choice for fig. Figs fruit and firm up best on a wet-then-dry cycle and dislike a root zone held constantly moist by a reservoir, which can invite root problems and, near harvest, split fruit. Figs are more forgiving of moisture than stone fruit, so a self-watering pot is workable in a pinch, but a freely draining pot you water yourself gives better fruit.

beginner: Protecting a potted fig in winter mostly means moving it somewhere sheltered, because the roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground. Put the resting, leafless plant in an unheated garage or shed for the coldest months. If it has to stay outside, push the pots together against a wall, wrap them, and pile mulch around them to keep the roots from freezing.
seasoned: Cold protection for a potted fig is mostly about moving it: the exposed pot lets roots freeze several zones colder than in the ground, so shelter the dormant plant in an unheated garage or shed through the coldest months. If it must stay outside in a marginal zone, cluster pots against a wall, wrap them, and bank mulch around them. The goal is a cold, stable dormancy without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots and top growth.

beginner: Figs are very perishable and do not ripen after you pick them, so pick them ripe and eat them quickly. On the counter ripe figs last only about a day or two before they go bad, so eat, cook, or refrigerate them the same day you pick.
seasoned: Figs are highly perishable and do not ripen further once picked, so pick them fully ripe and eat them fast. At room temperature ripe figs hold only about a day, sometimes two, before they begin to spoil, so plan to eat, cook, or refrigerate them the day you pick.

beginner: Put ripe figs in the fridge unwashed, in a single layer so they do not crush, and eat them within about 2 to 3 days. Let them warm up to room temperature before eating for the best taste.
seasoned: Refrigerate ripe figs unwashed in a single layer and use them within about 2 to 3 days. Cold slows the spoilage but figs are fragile; keep them shallow so they do not crush, and bring them to room temperature before eating for the best flavor.

beginner: Figs freeze nicely whole or cut in half. Rinse and dry them, freeze them on a tray, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for several months and are great for cooking and jam. Figs also dry very well, which is the traditional way to save a big crop.
seasoned: Figs freeze well whole or halved. Rinse, dry, and freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags; they keep several months and are best for cooking, baking, and preserves. Figs also dry excellently, the classic way to keep a big crop.

beginner: The main thing to remember is that figs do not ripen after picking and spoil in a day or two, so pick them ripe and use them fast, or refrigerate, freeze, or dry them right away.
seasoned: The key with figs is that they do not ripen off the plant and spoil within a day or two, so ripeness at picking and speed to the table (or fridge, freezer, or drying rack) is everything.

beginner: All common figs need about the same small amount of winter cold, so you do not pick a fig by chill hours the way you would a peach. Instead, choose by how cold-hardy it is and how well it handles your weather. In cold areas, pick a hardy type like Chicago Hardy or Celeste. In humid areas, pick a small, tight-eye type like Celeste or a rust-tolerant one like LSU Purple to avoid souring and rust. Where it is mild and dry, almost any fig does well, so pick by taste. All of these are common figs that fruit on their own with no pollination.
seasoned: Because all common figs need only about 100 chill hours, choose a variety not by chill (as you would a peach) but by cold-hardiness, disease tolerance, and eye type for your climate. In cold-winter areas favor the hardiest types (Chicago Hardy, Celeste, Marseilles). In humid areas favor a small, closed-eye variety (Celeste) or a rust-tolerant one (LSU Purple) to limit souring and rust. In mild, dry regions almost anything thrives, so pick by flavor and use. All the recommended types are common (parthenocarpic) figs that fruit alone with no pollination.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to fig. You plant it as a dormant bare-root or potted plant, so there is no tender young seedling to ease outside.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to fig. It is planted as a dormant, own-rooted bare-root or container plant, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate.

beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root or potted fig in late winter or early spring after the worst cold, or in fall to early winter where winters are mild.
